newsitem.title: USA: Clinton administration pushing new child tax plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton administration pushing new child tax plan.

text.p: The Clinton administration Friday proposed a new type of child tax credit under which lower-income families who do not pay taxes would receive money from the government.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said the proposal "would retain the child tax credit and would have an option to roll that over into some sort of savings vehicle for education."
The proposal would be more costly than President Clinton's original proposal for fiscal 1998 because that plan would not have given the credit to families who did not pay taxes.
Families would receive the tax credit for each child under age 13. It is aimed at helping families with child-related costs, but there is nothing to guarantee where the money would be spent.
The new plan was expected to raise the cost to the federal government of the child credit proposal to about $75 billion over five years, from about $47 billion for Clinton's initial proposal.

The new proposal would also allow families to contribute the child credit to an Individual Retirement Account (IRA) vehicle aimed at encouraging savings for the child. Interest earned on the child credit contribution to that account would be tax free.
After the first five years, families with children under age 18 would be eligible for the tax credit.

Like Clinton's original proposal, the new plan would start at $300 for each child under age 13 for 1998 and 1999 and increase to $500 in 2000. Taxpayers with incomes above $75,000 would not be eligible.
The administration has been working with two Democratic senators who have similar proposals.

One of those senators, Sen. Robert Kerrey of Nebraska, has a proposal called "KidSave" that would provide a $250 per child tax credit up to age 18 and would be increased to $500 if that amount was contributed in the child's name to an IRA-type account.

Rubin said the administration's new proposal improved the earlier child tax credit plan because it "makes it work better for low income people; and secondly by attaching to it a savings piece, in effect an IRA-like piece ... for education, you are also encouraging savings and providing for different resources for education."
Asked if the new proposal was now the administration's preference over the original, Rubin replied: "Yes, that's the thought that we are currently talking to people about."
The House tax-writing committee chairman is currently putting together a tax bill within the broad parameters of an $85 billion net tax cut over five years.

House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, planned to work over the weekend to complete the details of the tax bill, which was expected to be presented to the full committee Wednesday.
